units.subject: Physics
units.title: Position, Distance and Displacement
objectives: Distinguish scalar distance from vector displacement and calculate net displacement.
units.body:
Position locates an object relative to a chosen origin. Distance is total path length, a scalar with magnitude only. Displacement is the change from initial to final position, a vector with magnitude and direction. Its magnitude is the straight-line separation of the endpoints and cannot exceed the distance travelled. A journey can involve a large distance but zero displacement if the object returns to its starting point. For motion in two dimensions, resolve movements into perpendicular components and find the resultant displacement.

For vector quantities, show direction and use a consistent sign convention. Diagrams should be labelled and should distinguish measured quantities, directions and reference points. units.subject: Physics
units.title: Scalar and Vector Quantities
objectives: Classify physical quantities as scalars or vectors.
Represent vectors and calculate resultants and components.
units.body:
A scalar is completely described by magnitude and unit; examples include mass, time, distance, speed, temperature and energy. A vector requires magnitude and direction; examples include displacement, velocity, acceleration, force and momentum. A vector is represented by a directed line segment whose length represents magnitude and arrowhead indicates direction. Add vectors by triangle or parallelogram methods. For perpendicular components, Vx = V cos(theta) and Vy = V sin(theta); add components algebraically before finding the resultant.

For every calculation, write the known quantities with SI units, select a relation that contains the required unknown, substitute values with units, and check the dimensions of the result. For vector quantities, show direction and use a consistent sign convention. Diagrams should be labelled and should distinguish measured quantities, directions and reference points. practice.question: Two forces, whose resultant is 100 N, are perpendicular to each other. If one of them makes an angle of 60 degrees with the resultant, calculate its magnitude.

practice.answer: Resolving the two perpendicular forces parallel and perpendicular to the resultant gives force components of 50 N and 86.6 N. units.subject: Physics
units.title: Equations of Linear Motion and Motion Under Gravity
objectives: Apply equations of uniformly accelerated motion and interpret velocity-time graphs.
units.body:
Speed is the rate of change of distance; velocity is the rate of change of displacement; acceleration is the rate of change of velocity. For constant acceleration use v = u + at; s = ut + 1/2 at^2; v^2 = u^2 + 2as; and s = (u+v)t/2. A velocity-time graph has gradient equal to acceleration and signed area equal to displacement. For motion in stages, calculate each interval separately. In vertical motion under gravity, use g downward and maintain a consistent sign convention.

practice.question_locator: First-Term Physics source, Week 3 CLASSWORK, lorry motion problem.
practice.question: A lorry starts from rest and accelerates to 50 m/s in 10 s, travels at that speed for 15 s, then comes to rest uniformly in 5 s. Calculate acceleration, retardation, total distance and average speed.
practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not attributed to the source.
practice.answer: Acceleration = 5 m/s^2; retardation magnitude = 10 m/s^2. Distances are 250 m, 750 m and 125 m; total = 1,125 m. Total time = 30 s, so average speed = 37.5 m/s.
practice.explanation: Use areas under the velocity-time graph for the three stages.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Projectile Motion and Its Applications
objectives: Describe horizontal and vertical components of projectile motion.
Calculate time of flight, maximum height and range.
units.body:
A projectile moves under gravity after launch, neglecting air resistance. Its horizontal and vertical motions are independent. Horizontal velocity remains constant; vertical velocity changes uniformly under gravity. For launch speed u at angle theta, ux=u cos(theta), uy=u sin(theta). For launch and landing at the same level, T=2u sin(theta)/g, H=u^2 sin^2(theta)/(2g), R=u^2 sin(2theta)/g. Maximum range on level ground occurs at 45 degrees. For a horizontal launch, initial vertical velocity is zero.

practice.answer_locator: Authored model answer; not attributed to the source.
practice.answer: T=2u sin(theta)/g = 2 x 20 x sin(60)/10 = 3.46 s approximately.
practice.explanation: Use the vertical component and return-to-same-level relation.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Newton's Laws of Motion, Momentum and Collision
objectives: State and apply Newton's three laws of motion.
Use impulse and conservation of linear momentum in collision problems.
units.body:
Newton's first law describes inertia; the second relates resultant force to rate of change of momentum and for constant mass gives F=ma; the third states that interacting bodies exert equal and opposite forces on each other, acting on different bodies. Momentum p=mv is a vector. Impulse Ft equals change in momentum. In an isolated system total momentum remains constant. Elastic collisions conserve momentum and kinetic energy; in inelastic collisions momentum is conserved but some kinetic energy changes form. If bodies stick together, use a common final velocity.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Equilibrium of Forces, Moments, Couples and Stability
objectives: Apply translational and rotational equilibrium conditions.
Calculate moments and couples and explain centre of gravity and stability.
units.body:
A body is in equilibrium when resultant force and resultant moment are zero. For parallel forces, total upward force equals total downward force. For rotational equilibrium, clockwise moments equal anticlockwise moments about the same point. Moment = force x perpendicular distance, measured in N m. A couple consists of two equal, parallel and opposite forces acting along different lines; its moment is one force multiplied by perpendicular separation. Centre of gravity is the point through which resultant weight acts. Stable bodies return after a small displacement, unstable bodies move farther away, and neutral bodies remain in the new position.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Simple Harmonic Motion, Energy and Resonance
objectives: Define SHM and relate displacement, velocity, acceleration, period and frequency.
Calculate speed and acceleration in SHM and explain resonance.
units.body:
Simple harmonic motion is oscillatory motion in which acceleration is proportional to displacement from equilibrium and directed towards equilibrium: a=-omega^2 x. Amplitude is maximum displacement; period T is time for one oscillation; frequency f=1/T; angular frequency omega=2pi f=2pi/T. Maximum speed is omega A and maximum acceleration is omega^2 A. Kinetic energy is maximum at equilibrium and potential energy at the extremes. Forced vibration occurs when an external periodic force drives a system; resonance occurs when driving frequency matches the natural frequency.

units.subject: Physics
units.title: Machines: Mechanical Advantage, Velocity Ratio and Efficiency
objectives: Define load, effort, mechanical advantage and velocity ratio.
Calculate work input/output and machine efficiency.
units.body:
A machine makes work easier by changing force magnitude or direction or the distance over which force acts. Load is the resisting force; effort is applied force. Mechanical advantage MA=load/effort. Velocity ratio VR=distance moved by effort/distance moved by load. Efficiency is useful work output divided by work input, expressed as a percentage; efficiency=(MA/VR)x100. Ideal machines have MA=VR and 100% efficiency. Real machines lose energy through friction and other effects. Work input=effort x effort distance; work output=load x load distance.
